OPS06-BP03 Define escalation paths
When an incident exceeds what the first responder can resolve,
    someone must decide who acts next and with what authority.
    Escalation paths define when to escalate, who to involve at each
    level, and which actions are pre-approved, so decisions happen fast
    and the right people engage.
Desired outcome:
Your escalation paths move incidents to the right people
        quickly, with no confusion about who to involve next.
Your on-call responders hold the permissions and tools they need
        to act the moment they are paged.
You pre-approve high-impact actions for anticipated scenarios,
        so responders do not wait for sign-off during an incident.
Your stakeholders and customers receive updates in line with
        their expectations.
Common anti-patterns:
Teams lack clear recovery procedures, so responders improvise
        during critical incidents.
No one holds defined permissions or ownership, which delays
        action when speed matters most.
Stakeholders and customers learn about incidents late, out of
        step with expectations.
High-impact decisions, such as how to mitigate customer impact,
        wait on approvals that were never arranged in advance.
Benefits of establishing this best
    practice:
Incident response follows a predefined path, which removes
        hesitation at each hand-off.
Downtime shrinks because pre-approved actions and clear
        ownership let responders act immediately.
Support levels adjust to incident severity, so resources match
        the size of the problem.
Stakeholders and customers stay informed throughout the
        incident.
Level of risk exposed if this best practice
    is not established:
Medium
Implementation guidance
A first responder handles what they can, but some incidents need
      deeper expertise, wider authority, or a decision that carries
      business risk. An escalation path is the pre-agreed structure that
      moves an incident to the person who can act, at the moment the
      current responder reaches their limit. Without it, incidents stall
      while people work out who to call.
During an incident, decision authority is the scarce resource. A
      responder who knows the fix but lacks permission — or must wait
      for an executive to approve a customer-impacting action — loses
      minutes. Pre-approving actions for anticipated scenarios removes
      this bottleneck. You accept a small risk of a pre-authorized
      action being wrong in exchange for acting fast on foreseeable
      cases. Set these boundaries with decision-makers before an
      incident.
An escalation path must reach a person who can act. Name a role on
      the on-call schedule so the path stays valid when the current
      holder is unavailable. Each contact needs the permissions and
      access to act the moment they are engaged. Match the schedule
      depth to incident severity.
Many incidents depend on parties outside your team. Vendors,
      service providers, and other internal teams each have their own
      response times and contacts. Build those into the path. Document
      the service-level agreements (SLAs) you rely on, align them with
      your recovery goals, and keep vendor escalation contacts current
      and reachable. Stakeholders and customers expect timely updates,
      so decide who informs them, and how often, before the incident.
AWS DevOps Agent
can
investigate an incident autonomously
while the escalation proceeds,
      correlating telemetry, logs, and change history into a root-cause
      summary with recommended mitigations. The person engaged then
      starts with context and a proposed course of action.
An escalation path that is never exercised tends to break on first
      use. Rehearse through drills and game days so responders practice
      the process and gaps surface while the stakes are low. After each
      real incident, review how the path performed and refine it,
      because org charts, vendors, and workloads change.
Implementation steps
Set up escalation
            triggers:
Configure
CloudWatch alarms
to open a tracked work item when a monitored
            condition breaches its threshold. Create an
OpsItem in AWS Systems Manager OpsCenter
so the response is
            tracked from the outset, and route the alarm to the paging
            tool your organization uses so the right responder is
            notified.
Create on-call schedules:
Maintain on-call schedules in the paging tool your
            organization already runs, such as
Opsgenie
or
PagerDuty
.
            Name a role rather than a single person so the schedule
            stays valid when a responder is unavailable, and give
            on-call responders the permissions and tools to act the
            moment they are engaged.
Define escalation
            procedures:
Set the conditions under which an
            incident escalates, and capture them in the escalation
            policies of your paging or IT service management tool, such
            as
Opsgenie
,
PagerDuty
,
ServiceNow
,
            or
Jira Service Management
. Route each level to a contact or
            an on-call schedule, and state the roles and
            responsibilities at each tier.
Pre-approve mitigation
            actions:
Work with decision-makers to pre-approve
            actions for anticipated scenarios, and attach
Systems Manager Automation runbooks
to the
OpsItem
so responders run those actions quickly during an incident.
Assign ownership:
Name an
            internal owner for each step of the escalation path, so
            every stage of an incident has a named owner accountable for
            moving it forward.
Plan third-party
            escalations:
Document the SLAs you depend on and
            align them with your recovery goals. Set clear protocols for
            vendor communication, integrate vendor contacts into your
            incident tooling for direct access, and keep escalation
            information current and easy to find. Include third-party
            scenarios in your drills.
Train and rehearse escalation
            plans:
Train your team on the process, and run
            regular incident response drills or game days so the path
            works under pressure.
Review and improve:
Review the effectiveness of your escalation paths on a
            regular cadence, and update them based on lessons from
            post-incident analysis and ongoing feedback.
